say.text: Welcome to your very first class! I'll assume you know nothing yet, and that's perfect. Nothing is graded today. Just listen, and say each word back to me. Tap Next whenever you're ready, and tap any word to hear it again.
Spanish uses the same alphabet as English, plus one extra letter, ñ. Tap any letter to hear its Spanish name.
Spanish has just five vowel sounds, and they never change. A as in father, E as in bed, I as in see, O as in oh, and U as in food. Keep them short and pure.
A few letters sound different from English. H is always silent. J sounds like a strong, breathy h. Ñ sounds like the n y in canyon. And a double r is rolled.

The little line over a vowel is an accent mark. It shows which syllable to stress. Papá, with the accent, means dad. It can also tell two words apart: sí with an accent means yes, and si without one means if.
Now your first greeting: hola, hello. The h is silent, so it sounds like oh-la. Listen, and say it back to me.

rules.title: El and la: every noun is masculine or feminine

body.text: Every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine, and "the" changes to match: el for masculine, la for feminine.
Words ending in -o are usually masculine and words ending in -a usually feminine, but learn each noun with its el or la.

why.text: Spanish comes from Latin, which sorted every noun into groups. The groups stayed, so the little words around a noun (el, la, un, una) still show which group it's in.

body.text: The verb ending already tells you who is doing it, so Spanish usually leaves out the subject.
Es mi hermano means "he is my brother", and tengo means "I have". You only add él, ella or yo for emphasis.

why.text: The verb's ending already says who is doing it (hablo can only be 'I speak'), so saying yo too is like saying it twice. You add it only for emphasis or contrast.

rules.title: Adjectives go after the noun and match it

body.text: Describing words usually come after the noun: la casa blanca, "the white house".
They also match the noun: pequeño becomes pequeña for a feminine noun, and both add -s in the plural. Adjectives ending in -e, like grande, stay the same for both.

why.text: In Spanish the noun comes first and the description follows, so you hear what it is before you hear what it's like. The ending matches so it's clear which noun it describes.

body.text: Where English says "I am hungry", Spanish says "I have hunger": tengo hambre. The same goes for being sleepy, thirsty, cold or a certain age.

why.text: Spanish treats hunger, thirst, cold and fear as things you have, not states you are in. It's just a different picture of the same feeling.

rules.title: Culture: greetings in Spain and Latin America

body.text: Spain: two kisses on the cheek (right, then left) when women meet anyone; men usually shake hands with each other. Colombia, Mexico and most of Latin America: one kiss on the right cheek. In Argentina, men who are friends kiss on the cheek too.
Always greet when you walk into a small shop, a lift or a waiting room: "¡Buenos días!" or just "¡Buenas!". Asking for something without greeting first sounds cold.
In Colombia, usted is warm, not just formal: many people use it with friends and family. In Spain, tú comes quickly, even with strangers your age.
Gestures: Colombians often point with their lips. In Mexico and Colombia, show a person's height with your hand sideways; a flat palm facing down is for animals.

why.text: Greetings show respect and closeness, and each country settled on its own habits (one kiss, two kisses, a handshake), so it helps to watch what people do.

rules.title: Me levanto: verbs you do to yourself

body.text: Some verbs take me, te or se because you do them to yourself: levantarse (to get up), ducharse (to shower), vestirse (to get dressed).
The little word goes before the verb: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta.

why.text: With these verbs you do the action to yourself, so the little word me, te or se shows that you are both the one acting and the one it happens to.

body.text: For a finished action in the past, use the preterite. Regular -ar verbs end in -é for "I" (hablé), and -er / -ir verbs in -í (comí).
Ir (to go) and ser (to be) share the same past forms: fui means both "I went" and "I was".

why.text: The preterite presents an action as finished, with a clear start and end: it happened, it's done. That's why it's the tense for events.

rules.title: Culture: meals in Spain and Latin America

body.text: Spain eats late: lunch around 2 to 4 p.m. and dinner from 9 p.m. In Colombia and Mexico lunch, around noon to 2, is the big meal (the "menú del día" or "corrientazo" is a cheap set lunch), and dinner is lighter, around 7.
The waiter won't bring the check until you ask for it: lingering is normal. Say "¡Buen provecho!" to people who are eating, even other diners as you walk out.
Tips: in Colombia the bill often asks "¿Desea incluir el servicio?", an optional 10%. In Mexico leave 10 to 15%; in Spain, rounding up is enough.
Food words change: juice is "jugo" in Latin America and "zumo" in Spain; potato is "papa" and "patata".

why.text: Meals are social times in the Spanish-speaking world, which is why their timing and rituals matter more than in places where people eat on the go.

rules.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event

body.text: Spanish uses the imperfect to set the scene: what was going on, what used to happen (vivía, caminaba). It uses the preterite for the event that happened (encontró).
Think of the imperfect as the background and the preterite as the action.

why.text: Spanish uses one past for the background (what was going on: the imperfect) and another for the events that move the story forward (the preterite). Together they paint a scene.

why.text: Había plus a past participle puts one past event before another, exactly like English 'had done'. It helps you order events in a story.

rules.title: Me duele: pain works like gustar

body.text: Me duele means "it hurts me": the body part is the subject, with el or la instead of "my". For two body parts, use duelen.
Desde (since) with the present says how long something has been going on: tengo fiebre desde ayer.

why.text: Doler works like gustar: the thing that hurts is the subject. Me duele la cabeza is literally 'the head hurts me'.

rules.title: Giving advice: deberías, yo que tú, and the subjunctive

body.text: Deberías + verb is "you should". Yo que tú ("if I were you") takes the conditional: iría, diría.
After phrases like te recomiendo que or es importante que, the next verb goes into the subjunctive, which swaps the vowel of the ending: duermes becomes duermas, tomas becomes tomes.

why.text: Advice is about things that haven't happened yet, so Spanish uses the conditional (deberías) or the subjunctive, the mood for wishes and possibilities.

"Ahorita" can mean now, soon or not today. Social plans often start late, but work meetings start on time.

body.text: Aunque + the normal present states a fact: aunque es difícil (although it is hard).
Aunque + the subjunctive makes it hypothetical or concedes the point: aunque sea difícil, vale la pena (even if it's hard, it's worth it).

why.text: Aunque with the indicative states a fact ('although it is raining'). With the subjunctive it imagines a possibility ('even if it rains'). The mood carries the difference.

body.text: Usted is for people you don't know, older people, customers and formal situations. Tú is for friends, family and people your age.
In Colombia usted is also used warmly between friends and family, so you'll hear it everywhere. When unsure, start with usted and switch if the other person asks: ¿nos podemos tutear?

why.text: Spanish has two 'you's to show the relationship: tú is close and casual, usted keeps respect. Colombia uses usted a lot, even with friends and family.

body.text: The conditional (podría, sería, agradecería) softens any request.

why.text: Wrapping a request in a conditional or a question gives the other person room to say no, which is what makes it sound polite.

why.text: Mamar gallo is affectionate teasing: it shows you're close enough to joke, so taking it well is part of fitting in.

body.text: An idiom means something different from its words. Estar en las nubes, 'to be in the clouds', means to be daydreaming.
Learn each idiom as one block, with a situation to use it in. Change only the verb for the person: estás en las nubes, estoy en las nubes.

why.text: Idioms are pictures a language has kept for centuries. Their meaning comes from the picture, not the single words, so translating word by word doesn't work.

body.text: Colombian slang like parce (buddy), chévere (cool) and bacano (great) is friendly and casual. Use it with friends, not at a job interview.
Many reactions are short and fixed: ¡De una! means 'sure, let's do it', ¡Qué pena! means 'how embarrassing' or 'sorry'.

why.text: Slang grows in a community and marks belonging, so it changes from country to country and signals that you're among friends.

rules.title: Telling a story: the linking phrases

body.text: Good storytellers guide the listener. Resulta que, 'it turns out that', introduces the twist. Total que, 'so in the end', sums it up.
Y para colmo, 'and to top it off', adds the last straw, and al fin y al cabo, 'after all', wraps up.

why.text: These phrases tell the listener where the story is going: a twist, a summary, an ending. They keep people following, which makes a story feel natural.

intro.text: These lines come up in the role-play “Negotiating your salary”. Hear them now, so you know them before it's your turn.

lines.text: Nos encantaría que se uniera al equipo. La oferta es de cuatro millones al mes.
lines.en: We'd love for you to join the team. The offer is four million a month.

lines.text: Muchas gracias, me alegra mucho. Sin embargo, esperaba algo más cercano a los cinco millones.
lines.en: Thank you very much, I'm really pleased. However, I was hoping for something closer to five million.

lines.text: Entiendo. ¿En qué basa esa cifra?
lines.en: I understand. What do you base that figure on?

lines.text: En mi experiencia y en lo que se paga en el mercado por un cargo similar.
lines.en: On my experience and on what the market pays for a similar position.

lines.text: Podríamos llegar a cuatro millones y medio, más un día de trabajo remoto a la semana.
lines.en: We could go up to four and a half million, plus one day of remote work a week.

lines.text: Me parece razonable. ¿Podríamos revisarlo en seis meses?
lines.en: That seems reasonable. Could we review it in six months?

lines.text: Claro que sí. Lo dejamos por escrito en el contrato.
lines.en: Of course. We'll put it in writing in the contract.

body.text: Family matters a lot, and meeting your partner's family can happen fairly early, often at a Sunday lunch.
Use usted with your partner's parents until they tell you to use tú, and bring something small: dessert, pastries or flowers.
Offering to help clear the table always goes down well.

why.text: Family is central in Colombia, so meeting the family is a sign that someone is serious, and making a good impression on them matters.

lines.text: ¡Qué alegría tenerte aquí! Por fin te conocemos.

lines.text: Muchas gracias por invitarme, señora. Les traje un postre.

lines.text: ¡Ay, no te hubieras molestado! Siéntate, siéntate.
lines.en: Oh, you shouldn't have! Sit down, sit down.

lines.text: Es un placer. Andrés me ha hablado maravillas de su sazón.

lines.text: Este muchacho exagera. Bueno, cuéntame, ¿cómo se conocieron?

lines.text: ¡Qué bonito! Bueno, a comer, que se enfría el ajiaco.
lines.en: How lovely! Well, let's eat before the ajiaco gets cold.

body.text: Being direct about liking someone is fine, and asking for their number is normal. A "no" or a vague answer should be taken gracefully.
If you misread the situation, a simple apology and a friendly exit ("fue un gusto charlar contigo") leaves everyone comfortable.
Good-morning messages like "¿cómo amaneciste?" are a sweet, common way to show interest by text.

why.text: Being clear and kind at the same time protects the other person's feelings, which matters in a culture where politeness is highly valued.
